'''''Erythrostemon gilliesii''''' is a shrub in the [[Fabaceae|legume family]]. It is commonly known as '''bird of paradise''', but it is not related to the bird of paradise genus ''[[Strelitzia]]''.

==Description==
''Erythrostemon gilliesii'' is a large evergreen shrub with 2-pinnate leaves.<ref>[https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/379179/erythrostemon-gilliesii/details  Royal Horticultural Society website, ''Erythrostemon gilliesii'']</ref> It is upright, open, and rounded with yellow flowers and long crimson stamens.<ref name=TB>[https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/erythrostemon-gilliesii/  North Carolina Plant Toolbox website, ''Erythrostemon gilliesii'']</ref>

This plant grows up to 5m (16.5 ft), depending on rainfall.<ref>[https://invasives.org.za/fact-sheet/bird-of-paradise-flower/  Invasive Plants of South Africa website, ''Bird of Paradise flower'']</ref> The leaves are bipinnate, {{cvt|10|-|15|cm|0}} long, bearing 3–10 pairs of pinnae, each with 6–10 pairs of leaflets {{cvt|5|-|6|mm}} long and {{cvt|2|-|4|mm}} broad. The [[flowers]] are borne in [[raceme]]s up to {{cvt|20|cm|0}} long, each flower with five yellow petals with 10 long conspicuous red [[stamen]]s. The pods are densely covered in short, red glandular hairs.

==Cultivation==
 
It is a striking [[ornamental plant]] native to South [[Americas|America]], mainly [[Argentina]] and [[Uruguay]].<ref name=TB /><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Erythrostemon gilliesii (Hook.) Klotzsch {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:494656-1#distributions |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref><ref>[https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/CAEGI  EPPO Global Database website, ''Caesalpinia gilliesii'']</ref> It is naturalized in [[Texas]], and fairly common in the rest of the southwestern United States,<ref name=":0" /> where it is known as '''bird of paradise bush''', '''desert bird of paradise''', '''yellow bird of paradise''', and '''barba de chivo'''.

Although it is a tropical plant adapted to dry climates, it also thrives in the climate of [[Avsa]] and neighboring islands in the south of [[Sea of Marmara]] in northwestern [[Turkey]], where it is commonly known as '''Paşabıyığı''' (Pasabiyigi), '''Cennetkuşu ağacı''' (Cennetkusu agaci), which in Turkish means "bird of paradise tree," and '''Bodurakasya''', which means "dwarf acacia". This species is also fairly common in the [[Karoo]] of [[South Africa]], and found in the [[Catalonia]]n and [[Valencia]]n regions of [[Spain]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gómez Bellver |first=Carlos |last2=Nualart |first2=Neus |last3=Ibáñez |first3=Neus |last4=Burguera |first4=Carles |last5=Álvarez |first5=Hilari |last6=López i Pujol |first6=Jordi |date=2019 |title=Noves dades per a la flora al·lòctona de Catalunya i del País Valencià |url=https://doi.org/10.2436/20.1502.01.2 |journal=Butlletí de la Institució Catalana d'Història Natural |issue=83 |pages=23–40 |doi=10.2436/20.1502.01.2 |issn=2013-3987}}</ref>

== Medicinal uses ==
Medicine men of peoples indigenous to the [[Amazon rainforest]] used this plant and the similar ''[[Caesalpinia pulcherrima]]'', which they called ''ayoowiri'', for curing [[fever]], sores, and [[cough]]. Four grams from the root is also said to [[Abortifacient|induce abortion]] in the first trimester of pregnancy.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.boston.com/news/education/higher/articles/2006/07/24/amazing_mystery/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110522202611/http://www.boston.com/news/education/higher/articles/2006/07/24/amazing_mystery/ | url-status=dead | archive-date=May 22, 2011 | title=Amazon mystery: A medicine man understood the secrets of this plant long before we did. How? | author=S. Allen Counter | date=2006-07-24 | work=The Boston Globe}}</ref> Research has indicated that the plant has anti-microbial effects.<ref>[https://www.researchgate.net/publication/351547160_Anti-microbial_effects_of_aqueous_and_methanolic_extracts_of_Erythrostemon_gilliesii      ResearchGate website, ''Anti-Microbial effects of aqueous and methanolic extracts of Erythrostemon gilliesii'', article by Vida Tafakori and Nasim Nasiri, published in Nova Biologica Reperta in January 2020]</ref> 

It may also be used in the extraction of contaminants from soil.<ref>[https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10889868.2022.2136132  Taylor & Francis website,  ''Humic acid reduces lead phytoextraction efficiency of Erythrostemon gilliesii'', article by Mohammadreza Abdollahpour et al, published in Bioremediation Journal in November 2022]</ref>

== Poisoning ==
Poisoning may occur with the seeds of this plant.<ref name="Shoemaker_1958">{{cite journal | vauthors = Shoemaker HA | title = Bird of Paradise seed poisoning | journal = J Okla State Med Assoc | pages = 659–660 | date = November 1958| volume = 51 | issue = 11 | pmid = 13599076 | doi = }}</ref> The seeds and the green seed pods of this plant are toxic, provoking severe vomiting and other abdominal symptoms.<ref>[https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Erythrostemon+gilliesii&redir=Caesalpinia+gilliesii  Useful Tropical Plants website, ''Erythrostemon gilliesii'']</ref>
